Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 1–2:

(p-64) (Surat al-Hajj is Meccan, except for six verses from "These are two adversaries" to "the path of the Praiseworthy." Its verses number seventy-eight.)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a thing tremendous.﴾ Its "shaking" of things is taken as a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), or it is the shaking of things within it, so it is attributed to it by a semantic attribution (idafa ma'nawiyya) with the implied "in" (taqdir fi), or it is the attribution of the verbal noun to the time-noun, treating it as if it were the object.

It is also said that it is a convulsion that will occur shortly before the sun rises from its west, and its attribution to the Hour is because it is one of its portents. ﴿A thing tremendous﴾: terrifying. He gave the reason for their command to be mindful of God (taqwa) by the awfulness of the Hour, so that they might picture it with their minds and know that nothing will protect them from it except clothing themselves in the garment of taqwa, so that they preserve their souls and guard against it by constant adherence to taqwa.

﴿On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she was nursing, and every pregnant woman will drop her load.﴾ This is a depiction of its terror. The pronoun refers to "convulsion" (zalzala), and "the Day" (yawma) is in the accusative governed by "will be distracted" (tadhhalu). It has been read as "tadhhalu" and "tudhhalu" (passive and active), meaning: the convulsion will distract her. Dhuhul is leaving something in bewilderment (dahsha). The intended meaning is to indicate that its terror is such that a woman who had put her nursing infant to her breast, when bewildered, pulls it away from her mouth and forgets it. "Ma" here is either a relative pronoun or a verbal (masdari) particle. ﴿And every pregnant woman will drop her burden﴾: her fetus. ﴿And you will see people as drunk﴾: as if they were drunk. ﴿But they are not drunk﴾: in reality. ﴿Yet the punishment of God is severe﴾: its terror overwhelms them to the extent that it takes away their reason and eliminates their discernment. It has been read "tara" from "urituka qa'iman" or "ruitu qa'iman," with "al-nas" in the accusative or nominative (as the substitute for the subject), and its feminine form is on the interpretation of the group, and its singular after its plural because all see the convulsion, whereas the effect of drunkenness is seen by each person on others. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "sukara" as in "atsha," treating drunkenness as an illness (ila al-suk r majra al-'ilal).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 3–4:

﴿And among people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge﴾. It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was a fierce disputer. He used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah," "The Qur'an is the fables of the ancients," and "There is no resurrection after death." It (the revelation) covers him and his like. ﴿And he follows﴾ in the dispute, or in his general affairs, ﴿every rebellious devil﴾ (shaytan marid), one stripped bare for corruption; its root meaning is "nakedness" (al-ʿury).

﴿It is decreed for him﴾, that is, upon the devil, ﴿that whoever takes him as a guardian (tawallahu)﴾, that is, follows him, ﴿then indeed he will mislead him﴾. The particle "anna" here (the pronoun being for the matter/affair, al-shan) functions either as the predicate of "man" or as its response (jawab). The meaning is: it is decreed upon him to mislead whoever takes him as a guardian, because he is created with that disposition. It has also been read with a fatha (fa-anna), on the supposition of "fa-sha'nuhu annahu yudilluhu" ("so his matter is that he misleads him"), not as a conjunction (ʿatf), because then it would come after the completion of the sentence. It has also been read with a kasra in both places (inna), either as a quotation of what was written (hikayat al-maktub), or by implying a verb of saying (idmar al-qawl), or by treating "al-kutub" as containing this meaning (tadmin al-kutub maʿnahu). ﴿And he guides him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾, by driving him toward that which leads to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 5:

﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾ regarding its possibility and that it is something within God's power. It is also read as "min al-ba'ath" with a vowel on the ʿayn, like "al-jalb" (the vocalization being the same as in "al-jalb"). ﴿Then indeed, We created you﴾ meaning: consider the beginning of your creation, for it will dispel your doubt, [for] indeed We created you ﴿from dust﴾, either by creating Adam from it, or from the foods from which the seminal fluid is formed. ﴿Then from a drop﴾ of seminal fluid, from the verb "nataf" (to pour), ﴿then from a clinging clot﴾, a piece of congealed blood, ﴿then from a lump of flesh﴾, a piece of flesh which, originally, is the amount that can be chewed, ﴿formed and unformed﴾: shaped, with no deficiency or defect in it, and unshaped, or complete and miscarried, or given form and unformed.

﴿That We may make clear to you﴾ through this gradual process, Our power and Our wisdom, and that what accepts change, decay and formation once can accept it again, and that He who is able to change it and shape it first is able to do so a second time. The object is omitted, as a hint that by these acts of His there becomes manifest of His power and wisdom what cannot be encompassed by mention. ﴿And We cause to remain in the wombs what We will﴾, that We cause it to remain, ﴿for an appointed term﴾, which is the time of delivery; its minimum is six months and its maximum four years. It is also read "wa-nuqirra" in the accusative, and likewise His saying ﴿Then We bring you forth as a child﴾, coordinated with "nubayyin" (we make clear), as if their creation were arranged for two purposes: to make His power clear, and to keep them in the wombs until they are born, grow up, and reach the age of responsibility. It is also read with "ya" (y) in the nominative and accusative, and "yuqirru" with "ya" — ﴿wa-nuqirru﴾ — from "qarartu al-ma'a" (I poured the water), when I poured it. ﴿Tifl﴾ (child) is a state (ḥal) treated as applying to each one, or to indicate the category, or because it is originally a verbal noun.

﴿Then that you may reach your full strength﴾, your perfection in power and intellect; "ashudd" is the plural of "shidda," like "an'um" is the plural of "ni'ma," as if it were a strength in matters. ﴿And among you is he who is taken in death﴾ at the attainment of full strength or before it. It is also read "yutawwa" or "yatawaffahu Allah ta'ala" (God, exalted is He, causes him to die). ﴿And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age﴾, which is decrepitude and senility. It is also read with the mīm (m) vowelless.

﴿So that he knows nothing after having known﴾: that he returns to his former state in the time of childhood, through feebleness of intellect and scarcity of understanding, so that he forgets what he knew and denies what he recognized. The verse is a second argument for the possibility of the Resurrection from what befalls a human being at his various ages of differing matters and contrary conditions, for whoever is able to do that is able to do its like. ﴿And you see the earth barren﴾, dead and dry, from "hamadat al-nar" when the fire becomes ashes. ﴿Then when We send down upon it water, it stirs﴾, moves with vegetation. ﴿And swells﴾ and expands. It is also read "wa-rabaʾat," meaning it rose. ﴿And it causes to grow of every lovely pair﴾, of every beautiful, good, pleasing kind. This is a third proof, which God repeated in His Book because of its manifestness and because it is witnessed.

﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned: the creation of man in various stages, his transformation through contrary states, and the reviving of the earth after its death. It is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is:

﴿That Allah is the Truth﴾, meaning: because He is the Established One in His own essence, through whom things are realized.

﴿And that He gives life to the dead﴾, and that He is able to bring them back to life, for otherwise He would not have brought to life the drop of semen and the dead earth.

﴿And that He is powerful over everything﴾, because His power belongs to His essence, and its relation to all things is equal. So when observation proved His power to revive some of the dead, it became necessary that He is capable of reviving all of them.(p-66)

﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it﴾, for change is among the precursors and early signs of its ending.

﴿And that Allah will raise up those who are in the graves﴾, in accordance with His promise, which does not admit of being broken.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 8–10:

﴿And among people is one who argues about God without knowledge﴾. This is a repetition for emphasis, and for the indication contained in his words: ﴿nor guidance, nor an illuminating Book﴾, to show that he has no basis, neither from reasoning (istidlal) nor from revelation (wahy). Alternatively, the first (phrase) refers to the imitators (al-muqallidin, those who follow others' opinions without independent evidence), and this (second phrase) refers to those who are imitated (al-muqallad). By "knowledge" is meant innate knowledge (al-'ilm al-fitri, the knowledge natural to human nature), so that the conjunction of ﴿guidance﴾ and ﴿Book﴾ with it is correct.

﴿turning aside in arrogance﴾. "Turning the side" (thani 'utfihi) is a metonymy (kinaya) for arrogance, with the neck held high. Or it means turning away from the truth, treating it with contempt.

It is also read with a fatha on the ʿayn, meaning: preventing his bending (to the truth). ﴿so that he may lead astray from the way of God﴾ is the reason for the disputing. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ruways read the yāʾ with a fatha, on the basis that his turning away from the guidance, which was within his reach, by devoting himself to vain disputation, is an exit from guidance into error, and that, in terms of its outcome, it is as though it were his aim. ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾, which is what befell him on the day of Badr. ﴿And We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the burning﴾, the burned, which is the Fire.

﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾. This is an iltifat (a shift from address to third person), or an implied "saying": that is, it will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection, "That disgrace and punishment is because of what you committed of disbelief and sins." ﴿And that God is not unjust to the servants﴾. Rather, He requites them for their deeds. The intensive form (ẓallām) is used because of the great number of servants.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 11:

﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge.﴾ On a fringe of religion, with no steadfastness in it, like one who stands at the edge of an army: if he senses victory he stays, and otherwise he flees. ﴿If good befalls him, he is reassured by it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face.﴾ It is related that it was revealed concerning Bedouins (a'arib) who came to Medina. When one of them was healthy in body, his mare foaled a sound colt, his wife bore a healthy boy, and his wealth and livestock increased, he would say: "Since I entered this religion of mine, I have only encountered good," and he was reassured. But if the matter was the opposite, he would say: "I have only encountered evil," and he turned back.

And on the authority of Abu Sa'id: "A Jew embraced Islam, then calamities befell him, so he blamed Islam for it (tasha'ama bil-Islam). He came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Release me from it (aqilni).' He [the Prophet] said: 'Indeed, Islam is not to be retracted (la yuqalu).'" Then it was revealed.

﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter.﴾ By the loss of his protection (ismah) and the nullifying (hubut) of his deeds through apostasy. It was read as "khasiran" in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (hal), and in the nominative, as the subject (fa'iliyyah). Placing the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to make clear his loss (tansis 'ala khusranihi), or it is a omitted predicate (khabar mahdhuf). ﴿That is the manifest loss.﴾ For there is no loss like it.

﴿It calls upon, besides Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him.﴾ He worships inanimate matter that can neither harm by itself nor benefit. ﴿That is the far-reaching error.﴾ "Far" from the goal is a metaphor drawn from the error of one who goes far astray in the wilderness.

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit.﴾ "Harm" is due to his being worshipped, since that entails killing in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. "Benefit" is what is expected from worshipping him, namely intercession and seeking nearness to God through it. The lam (اللام) is connected to (يدعو, "calls") insofar as it carries the sense of (يزعم, "claims"). Claiming (الزعم) is a statement accompanied by belief. Or the lam is introduced before a sentence that falls as the object of saying, treating it as if it were (يقول, "says"); that is, the disbeliever says this with calling out and shouting when he sees the harm he suffers from it. Or the clause is a new sentence, with (يدعو, "calls") repeating the first. In that case (من, "whoever") is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿Surely wretched is the patron﴾, meaning the helper, ﴿and surely wretched is the companion﴾, meaning the associate.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 22, verses 14–15:

﴿Indeed, Allah admits those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.﴾ This refers to the reward of the righteous monotheist and the punishment of the wicked polytheist, which none can repel or prevent.

﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the Hereafter...﴾ This is an elliptical statement. The meaning is: Allah will help His Messenger in this world and the Hereafter, so whoever thinks otherwise and expects the contrary out of his rage [is addressed]. It has also been said that "help" (al-nasr) here means provision (al-rizq), and the pronoun refers to "whoever" (man).

﴿Then let him stretch a rope to the sky, then let him cut [it off]...﴾ Let him exert himself to the utmost in removing his rage or distress, by doing everything that one filled with rage or extremely distressed would do, even to the point of stretching a rope to the ceiling of his house and hanging himself, from qata'a (to cut off), when one is choked, since the one being strangled cuts off his breath by obstructing its passages. It has also been said: let him stretch a rope to the lowest heaven, then let him cut through the distance with it until he reaches its vault, and strive to repel his help or to obtain his provision. Warsh, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "li-yaqta'" (﴿ليقطع﴾) with a kasra on the lam. ﴿Then let him look﴾ means: let him imagine within himself.

﴿Will his scheme remove what enrages him?﴾ His doing that is called a "scheme" according to the first interpretation, because it is the utmost of what he is capable of. ﴿What enrages him﴾ means his rage, or that which enrages him, namely the help of Allah. It has also been said that this was revealed concerning Muslims who were impatient for Allah's help, out of their haste and their intense rage against the polytheists.

﴿And thus﴾ like this sending down. ﴿We sent it down﴾ We sent down the Qur'an in its entirety. ﴿As clear signs﴾ evident. ﴿And that Allah guides﴾ and because Allah guides by it, or makes firm upon the guidance, ﴿whom He wills﴾ to His guidance or to its firmness; He sent it down thus, making things clear.

﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate partners [with Allah] — indeed Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ by ruling between them and manifesting the one of truth among them over the one of falsehood, or by recompense, so that He repays each one with what befits it and admits him to the place prepared for him. And "inna" was placed before each of the two parts of the sentence for the sake of additional emphasis. ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things a witness﴾ knowing of it, observing its circumstances.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 18:

﴿Do you not see that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ (meaning: they are subjugated to His power and do not hold back from His governance); or it indicates, through their humbleness, the greatness of the One who governs them. It is possible that "whoever" (man) is general, encompassing those endowed with intellect (ulu al-ʿaql) and others, by way of prioritizing the rational (al-taghlib), so that His saying: ﴿and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the animals﴾ is a singling out of them by mention because of their prominence and because prostration is considered unlikely from them. It was also recited "wa-l-dawabbu" with lightening (takhfif), out of disliking the doubling (taḍʿif) or the joining of two consonants with sukun (al-jamʿ bayna al-sakinayn). ﴿and many of mankind﴾ is conjoined to them (ʿuṭifa ʿalayhā), if it is permitted to employ a single word in each of its two meanings, and to ascribe it, with regard to one of them, to one matter and, with regard to the other, to another; for the specifying of "many" indicates the particular meaning ascribed to them. Or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, indicated by the predicate of its counterpart, such as "haqqun lahu al-thawab" (it is right that he has the reward). Or it is the agent of a verb implied, i.e., "and many of mankind prostrate to Him" in the prostration of obedience. ﴿and many have deserved the punishment﴾ because of their disbelief and their refusal to obey. It is permissible to make "and many" a repetition of the first for the sake of emphasis regarding the multitude of those deserving punishment, so that it is conjoined to those who prostrate in the general sense, described by what follows it. It was also recited "ḥaqqa" with a damma, and "ḥaqqan" with the verb implied. ﴿And whoever Allah humiliates﴾ with wretchedness, ﴿for him there is no honourer﴾ who honours him with felicity; it was also recited with a fatḥa, in the sense of honouring (al-ikram). ﴿Indeed Allah does whatever He wills﴾ of honouring and humiliating.

This is the commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 19–20:

﴿These two adversaries (hadhani khasmani)﴾ means two opposing groups (fawjani mukhtasimani). For this reason He said ﴿they dispute (ikhtasamu)﴾, taking it according to the sense (hamlan 'ala al-ma'na); had it been reversed, it would also have been permissible. By them is meant the believers and the disbelievers. ﴿Concerning their Lord﴾: concerning His religion, or concerning His essence and attributes. It has been said that the Jews and the believers disputed. The Jews said: "We have a better claim to God and are older than you in scripture, and our prophet came before your prophet." The believers said: "We have a better claim to God; we believe in Muhammad and your prophet and in what God has sent down of scripture, while you know our scripture and our prophet, yet you disbelieved out of envy." So this was revealed. ﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾: this is the decisive judgment (fasl) of their dispute, and it is what is meant by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾: they will be measured out for them according to the measures of their bodies; it is also read with the lighter form (bi-al-takhfif). ﴿Garments of fire﴾: fires that encompass them as garments encompass the body. ﴿Scalding water will be poured over their heads﴾: this is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "for them" or a second predicate (khabar thani), and al-hamim is hot water.

﴿Whereby what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted﴾: that is, its heat, by its intensity, affects their insides just as it affects their outsides, so their innards are melted by it just as their skins are melted. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (al-hamim) or from their pronoun. It is also read with the doubled form (bi-al-tashdid) for intensification.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 21–22:

﴿And for them are hooks of iron (maqami').﴾ They are whips made of it with which they are beaten. It is the plural of miqma'ah, and its literal meaning is that with which something is repressed (yuqma'), i.e., restrained forcefully.

﴿Every time they wish to come out of it﴾ — from the Fire. ﴿From distress﴾ — from its distresses. It is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun (in "minha"), with the preposition repeated. ﴿They will be returned to it﴾ — meaning, when they have come out, they are returned, because returning is only after coming out. It has also been said that the flame of the Fire strikes them and lifts them to its top, and then they are struck with the hooks and they fall back into it. ﴿And taste﴾ — meaning, it has been said, that it is said to them: taste. ﴿The punishment of the burning﴾ — i.e., the Fire that reaches the utmost in burning.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 23–24:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. He changed the style here, attributed the admission to Allah the Exalted, and emphasized it with "inna" (indeed), praising the condition of the believers and magnifying their station. ﴿They will be adorned therein﴾ from "halla'tu al-mar'ah" (I adorned the woman), meaning when I put jewelry on her; it is also read with the lighter form (yuhallawna), and the meaning is one. ﴿with bracelets﴾ is an adjective of an omitted object, and "asawir" is the plural of "aswira," which is the plural of "siwar" (bracelet). ﴿of gold﴾ is an explanation of it. ﴿and pearls﴾ is conjoined to it (the bracelets), not to "gold," because a bracelet is not known to be made of it except when it is meant to be set with it (i.e., studded with pearls). Nafi' and 'Asim put it in the accusative, conjoining it to the place of the preceding (or by supposing an implied governing verb, like "wa yu'tuna" [and they will be given]). Hafs narrated it with two hamzas; Abu Bakr and al-Susi, from Abu 'Amr, dropped the first hamza. It is also read "lu'lu'an" (changing the second hamza to waw), "lu'liyan" (changing both to waw, then the second to ya'), and "lili'yan" (changing both to ya'), and "lu'lun" like "adl." ﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾: he changed the style of the speech here to indicate that silk is their customary garments, or to preserve the form of the rhyme endings (fawasil).

﴿And they were guided to the good of speech﴾, which is their saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾, or the word of monotheism. ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾: "the Praiseworthy" is either Himself (the One praised), or His outcome, which is Paradise, or the Truth, or the One who by His very essence deserves praise, and He is Allah, glorified and exalted, and His path is Islam.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾ does not intend by it a present or future state. Rather, it intends the continuation of their obstruction, as in the saying "So-and-so gives and withholds." For this reason, its conjunction with the past tense is apt (ʿaṭf, grammatical coordination). It is also said that it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the subject of (kafarū), and the predicate of (inna) (indeed) is omitted, indicated by the end of the verse, meaning "they will be punished."

﴿and the Sacred Masjid﴾ is coordinated with the name of Allah. Al-Hanafiyyah interpreted it as Mecca, citing His saying: ﴿which We made for the people, equal for the one who resides in it and the visitor﴾, meaning the resident (al-muqīm) and the passerby (al-ṭāriʾ), as evidence against the permissibility of selling or renting its houses. This argument, despite its weakness, is opposed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿those who were expelled from their homes﴾, and by ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) buying the prison house in Mecca without objection.

(sawāʾan) is a predicate placed before its subject (khabar muqaddam), and the whole clause is a second object (mafʿūl thānī) of (jaʿalnāhu) (We made it), if (lilnnās) is made a ḥāl from the pronoun ha (it). Otherwise, it is a ḥāl from the implicit pronoun in (fīhi). Ḥafṣ read it in the accusative, as either the object or the ḥāl. (al-ʿākif) is nominative, being its subject. It was also read as (al-ʿākifi) in the genitive, as a substitute (badal) for (al-nās).

﴿and whoever intends therein﴾: its object has been omitted so that it encompasses every possible object. It was also read with a fatḥah, from (al-wurūd) (arriving). ﴿with deviation﴾ means turning away from the right course. ﴿with injustice﴾ means without right. These two are synonymous ḥāl clauses; or the second is a substitute (badal) for the first, with the preposition repeated, or it is a complement (ṣilah) to it, meaning: deviating by reason of injustice, such as associating partners with Allah and committing sins. ﴿We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ is the response (jawāb) to (man) (whoever).

And when We settled Abraham in the place of the House. That is: remember when We appointed it for him and made it a dwelling-place (mubaa'ah) for him. It has been said that the lam (ل) is superfluous (za'idah), and makan (مكان) is an adverbial of place (zarf), meaning: "and when We settled him in it." It has been said that the House was raised up to the heavens and effaced during the days of the Flood. So God informed him of its place by means of a wind He sent, which swept clean what was around it, and he built it upon its ancient foundation.

﴿That you associate nothing with Me, and purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stand, and bow and prostrate.﴾

Here (أن) is explanatory (mufassirah) for (بوأنا), inasmuch as it includes the meaning of (تعبدنا), "We made him worship," because settling him was for the sake of worship. Or it is a verbal particle (مصدرية) joined to the prohibition (لا تشرك), meaning: We did that so that you would not associate anything in My worship. "And purify My House of idols and filth for those who circle it and pray in it." Perhaps he expressed prayer (الصلاة) by its pillars (أركانها) to indicate that each one of them independently requires this, how much more so when they are combined.

It was read as (يُشْرَكْ) with a yā' (the third-person form). Nafi', Hafs and Hisham read (بيتيَ) with a fatha on the yā' (ياء).

(p-70)

﴿And proclaim among the people﴾: call out to them. It is also read as "wa-ādhin." ﴿of the pilgrimage﴾: by calling people to the pilgrimage (ḥajj) and commanding it.

It is narrated that he (ﷺ) ascended Abu Qubays and said: "O people, make the pilgrimage to the House of your Lord." God made his call audible from the loins of men and the wombs of women, between the East and the West, to everyone who was foreordained in His knowledge to make the pilgrimage.

It was also said that the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who was commanded to do this during the Farewell Pilgrimage (ḥajjat al-wadāʿ). ﴿They will come to you on foot﴾: ﴿rijālan﴾ is the plural of rājil (one who travels on foot), like qāʾim and qiyām. It is also read with a damma on the rāʾ, with the jīm lightened or doubled, and as "rajālā," like ʿajālā. ﴿And on every lean camel﴾: that is, riding on every emaciated camel that the distance of the journey has worn out and made lean. ﴿Coming﴾ (yaʾtīna) is an adjective of ﴿lean﴾ (ḍāmir), understood according to its meaning. It is also read as "yaʾtūna," as an adjective of the men and riders, or as a new independent clause, in which case the pronoun refers to ﴿the people﴾.

﴿From every deep pass﴾: from every path. ﴿Deep﴾: distant. It is also read as "maʿīq." It is said: "a well of great depth" (buʾr baʿīdat al-ʿumq), and al-ʿumq and al-maʿq have the same meaning.

﴿That they may witness﴾: that they may attend. ﴿Benefits for them﴾: religious and worldly. The word is indefinite because what is meant is a particular kind of benefit specific to this act of worship. ﴿And mention the name of God﴾: at the preparation of the offerings and sacrificial animals and at slaughtering them. It was also said that mention (dhikr) is used as a metaphor for sacrifice (naḥr), because the slaughter of Muslims is never separate from it, which draws attention to the fact that it is the purpose of what is offered to draw near to God, exalted is He. ﴿On known days﴾: these are the ten days of Dhu al-Ḥijja. It was also said they are the days of sacrifice (ayyām al-naḥr). ﴿Over what He has provided for them of livestock animals﴾: he attached the act to what is provided and specified it as livestock, to encourage drawing near (to God) and to draw attention to what the mention requires. ﴿So eat from them﴾: from their meat. He commanded this as a permission and a removal of what the people of pre-Islamic ignorance (jāhiliyya) considered sinful in it. It is also an recommendation (nadb) to share with the poor and to treat them equally. This applies to voluntary sacrifice, not to obligatory sacrifice.

﴿And feed the distressed﴾: the one who has been afflicted with bu's, that is, hardship. ﴿The poor﴾: the one in need. The command here is for obligation, though it has been said that this applies to the first (i.e., the distressed) as well.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 29–30:

﴿Then let them end their state of unkemptness﴾ i.e., let them remove their dirt by trimming the moustache and nails, plucking the armpit hair, and shaving the pubic hair at the time of ihlal (exiting the state of ihram).

﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾ i.e., what they vow of righteousness during their pilgrimage. It is also said that it refers to the obligatory duties of the Hajj. Abu Bakr recited it with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the fa' (wa-liyuwaffu / walyawwafu, i.e., walyawwafū). ﴿And let them circumambulate﴾ the circumambulation of the pillar (tawaf al-rukn), by which the exit from ihram is completed, for it accompanies the ending of the state of unkemptness. It is also said that it refers to the farewell circumambulation (tawaf al-wada'). Ibn 'Amir alone recited it with a kasra on the lam in both places (walyaṭṭawwafū and walyūfū). ﴿By the Ancient House﴾ the old one, because it is the first house established for people; or the one freed from the domination of tyrants, for many a tyrant has aimed at it to demolish it, and Allah prevented him. As for al-Hajjaj, he only intended to expel Ibn al-Zubayr from it, not to dominate over it.

﴿That﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., the matter is that; and this and its like are used to separate one speech from another. ﴿And whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah﴾ His commandments and everything whose violation is not permitted; or the sanctuary and what relates to the Hajj of obligations. It is also said: the Ka'bah, the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred City, the Sacred Month, and the forbidden month. ﴿It is better for him﴾ so honouring is better for him. ﴿With his Lord﴾ in reward.

﴿And the cattle have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you﴾ except that whose prohibition is recited to you, and that is what is forbidden of them due to an external cause, such as carrion and what has been dedicated to other than Allah. So do not forbid any of them other than what Allah has forbidden, like the bahira and the sa'iba. ﴿So shun the abomination of idols﴾ so shun the abomination which is the idols, as impurities are shunned; and this is the utmost emphasis in prohibiting their veneration and in repelling people from worshipping them.

﴿And shun the word of falsehood﴾ a generalisation after a specification, for worship of idols is the head of falsehood. It is as if, when he urged the honouring of the sacred rites, he followed it with this, as a refutation of what the disbelievers held regarding the forbidding of the bahira and sa'iba, the venerating of idols, and fabricating against Allah the Exalted that He had decreed all that. It is also said that it refers to false testimony, for it is reported that he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "False testimony is equal to associating partners with Allah," three times, and then recited this verse.

Al-zur is from al-zawr, which is deviation, just as al-ifk is from al-ifk, which is turning away, for falsehood is deviant and turned away from reality. (p-71)

Ibn 'Amir alone recited it with a kasra on the lam in both places (walyaṭṭawwafū and walyūfū). ﴿By the Ancient House﴾ the old one, because it is the first house established for people; or the one freed from the domination of tyrants, for many a tyrant has aimed at it to demolish it, and Allah prevented him. As for al-Hajjaj, he only intended to expel Ibn al-Zubayr from it, not to dominate over it.

﴿That﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., the matter is that; and this and its like are used to separate one speech from another. ﴿And whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah﴾ His commandments and everything whose violation is not permitted; or the sanctuary and what relates to the Hajj of obligations. It is also said: the Ka'bah, the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred City, the Sacred Month, and the forbidden month. ﴿It is better for him﴾ so honouring is better for him. ﴿With his Lord﴾ in reward.

﴿And the cattle have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you﴾ except that whose prohibition is recited to you, and that is what is forbidden of them due to an external cause, such as carrion and what has been dedicated to other than Allah. So do not forbid any of them other than what Allah has forbidden, like the bahira and the sa'iba. ﴿So shun the abomination of idols﴾ so shun the abomination which is the idols, as impurities are shunned; and this is the utmost emphasis in prohibiting their veneration and in repelling people from worshipping them.

﴿And shun the word of falsehood﴾ a generalisation after a specification, for worship of idols is the head of falsehood. It is as if, when he urged the honouring of the sacred rites, he followed it with this, as a refutation of what the disbelievers held regarding the forbidding of the bahira and sa'iba, the venerating of idols, and fabricating against Allah the Exalted that He had decreed all that. It is also said that it refers to false testimony, for it is reported that he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "False testimony is equal to associating partners with Allah," three times, and then recited this verse.

Al-zur is from al-zawr, which is deviation, just as al-ifk is from al-ifk, which is turning away, for falsehood is deviant and turned away from reality. (p-71)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 31–32:

﴿True in faith to Allah﴾, sincere to Him. ﴿Not associating anything with Him﴾: these two are circumstantial clauses (hal) relating to the waw (of the verb's subject). ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾, because he has fallen from the height of faith to the depth of disbelief. ﴿Then the birds snatch him away﴾, for base desires scatter his thoughts. Nafi' alone read ﴿fa-takhtafuhu﴾ with a fatha on the kha' and a shadda on the ta'. ﴿Or the wind throws him into a distant place﴾, far away, for Satan has cast him far astray into misguidance. The particle "aw" (or) here expresses choice (lil-takhyir), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or like a downpour from the sky﴾. Or it expresses variety (lil-tanwi'), for among the polytheists there is one for whom there is no deliverance at all, and among them there is one whose deliverance is possible through repentance, but from a distance. It is also permissible that this be among the compound similes, so the meaning becomes: whoever associates others with Allah, his soul has perished with a destruction resembling one of the two destructions.

﴿That, and whoever honors the rites of Allah﴾: the religion of Allah, or the obligations of the Hajj and its places of rituals, or the sacrificial animals, because they are among the landmarks of the Hajj. This last is the most consistent with what follows it. Honoring them means choosing them to be fine, fat, and of high price.

It is narrated that "he (ﷺ) (the Prophet) sent as an offering one hundred camels, among them a camel belonging to Abu Jahl, with a nose-ring of gold," and that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) offered a noble she-camel that was sought from him for three hundred dinars.

﴿For indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾: for honoring them is among the actions of those who possess piety of the heart. So these added elements and the pronoun referring back to "whoever" have been omitted. He mentioned the hearts because they are the source of piety and wickedness, or because they are what commands both of them.

For you there are benefits in them until a specified term; then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House. That is, for you there are benefits from them, their milk, offspring, wool and riding, until they are slaughtered. Then the time of their slaughter arrives, ending at the House, meaning the part of the sacred precinct (al-Haram) adjacent to it. That is, for you there are worldly benefits until the time of slaughter, and after that there are religious benefits, which are greater than them. According to the first two readings, this is either connected to the discussion of ﴿the livestock﴾, with the pronoun in ﴿فيها﴾ ("in them") referring to it, or, according to the first reading, the meaning is: for you there are religious benefits from which you profit until a specified term, which is death. Then their place is at the Ancient House, to which deeds are raised, or in which their reward is kept, and that is the Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) or Paradise. According to the second reading, for you there are benefits of trade in the markets until the time of return. Then the time of leaving them ends at the Ka'bah, by exiting the state of ihram through the tawaf of visitation (ṭawāf al-ziyārah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 34–35:

﴿And for every community﴾ — for every people of a religion. ﴿We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾ — a means of worship, or a sacrifice by which they draw near to God. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra (mansik), meaning a place of rites (nusuk). ﴿That they may mention the name of God﴾ — alone, to the exclusion of others, and direct their sacrifice to His face. He gave the reason for the appointing with this, as an alert that the purpose of the rites is the remembrance of the One worshipped. ﴿Over what He has provided for them of the livestock of cattle﴾ — at the time of slaughtering them. In this there is an indication that the sacrifice must be of the cattle (in'am).

﴿So your God is one God, so submit to Him﴾ — make your drawing near or remembrance sincere, and do not mix it with associating partners.

﴿And give good tidings to the humble (mukhbitin)﴾ — the humble or the sincere, for humility (ikhbat) is their attribute.

﴿Those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned﴾ — out of awe of Him, due to the shining of the rays of His majesty upon them. ﴿And those who endure patiently what befalls them﴾ — of hardships and calamities. ﴿And those who establish the prayer﴾ — at its appointed times. It was also read as "wal-muqimina as-salah" (the accusative plural, muqimina), according to the original form.

﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾ — in the ways of good.

The camels (﴿وَالْبُدْنَ﴾): the plural of *badanah*, like *khushub* and *khashabah*. Its original vowelling is with a *ḍammah* (بُدْن), and it has been recited that way. The camel was called *badanah* because of the largeness of its body (*badan*), derived from *badana*, *badanah* (to become stout). The fact that the cow shares with it the rule of being counted as sufficient for seven people, according to his saying ﷺ, "The camel is for seven and the cow is for seven," does not necessarily mean that the name *badanah* applies to the cow in the Law. Rather, the hadith prevents that. Its being in the accusative (*intiṣāb*) is by a verb that explains it (i.e., a verb implied and interpreted by the following clause).

﴿جَعَلْنَاهَا لَكُمْ﴾: "We have made them for you." Whoever reads it in the nominative makes it a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence).

﴿مِنْ شَعَائِرِ اللَّهِ﴾: "from among the rites of God," meaning from among the signs of His religion which God has legislated.

﴿لَكُمْ فِيهَا خَيْرٌ﴾: "there is good for you in them," meaning religious and worldly benefits.

﴿فَاذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهَا﴾: "then mention the name of God over them," by saying at the time of slaughtering them: "God is greatest, there is no god but God, and God is greatest. O God, from You and to You."

﴿صَوَافَّ﴾: "standing," meaning standing with their forelegs and hind legs arranged in line. It has also been recited as *ṣawāfin* (صَوَافِنَ), from *ṣafana al-faras* (the horse stood on three legs with the tip of the hoof of the fourth leg touching the ground), because the camel is tied so that one of its forelegs is bound and it stands on three. It has also been recited as *ṣawāfinan* (صَوَافِنًا), with the *tanwīn* replaced by the vowel of pause (*ḥarf al-iṭlāq*) when stopping. And *ṣawāfiya* (صَوَافِيَ), meaning purely for the sake of God's countenance. And *ṣawāfī* (صَوَافِي) with the *yā'* sukūn, according to the dialect of those who make the *yā'* quiescent in all cases, as in their saying: *a'ṭi al-qawsa bārīhā* (give the bow to its maker).

﴿فَإِذَا وَجَبَتْ جُنُوبُهَا﴾: "then when their sides fall," meaning they fall to the ground, and this is a metaphor (*kināyah*) for death.

﴿فَكُلُوا مِنْهَا وَأَطْعِمُوا الْقَانِعَ﴾: "So eat from them and feed the contented one," meaning the one who is satisfied with what he has and with what is given to him without asking. This is supported by the recitation *al-qunua'* (القُنُعَ). Or it means the one who asks, from *qanaʿtu ilayhi qunūʿan*, when I humbled myself to him in asking.

﴿وَالْمُعْتَرَّ﴾: "and the one who presents himself (for charity) without asking," that is, the one who approaches with a request. It has been recited as *al-mu'tarī* (وَالْمُعْتَرِي). It is said: *arrahu*, *ʿarrāhu*, *iʿtarrahu* and *iʿtarāhu* (all meaning he came to him seeking).

﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾: "in this way," like what We have described of their slaughter while standing.

﴿سَخَّرْنَاهَا لَكُمْ﴾: "We have subjected them to you," despite their size and strength, so that you take them submissively, tie them, and restrain them with their legs arranged in line, and then you stab them in the chest.

﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ﴾: "that perhaps you may be thankful," for Our favour upon you, by drawing near (to God) and by sincerity.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 37:

﴿Their flesh will not reach God, nor their blood, but piety from you will reach Him.﴾ (Lan yanal Allah) means: it will not reach His good pleasure, nor will it be accepted from Him. ﴿Their flesh﴾ (luhumuha) refers to what is given in charity from it. ﴿Nor their blood﴾ (wa la dima'uha) refers to what is shed by slaughter, insofar as it is flesh and blood. ﴿But piety from you reaches Him﴾ (wa lakin yanaluhu al-taqwa minkum) means: but what reaches Him is the piety of your hearts that accompanies it, which calls you to magnify His command, to draw near to Him, and to be sincere toward Him. It has been said: the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era), when they slaughtered sacrificial offerings, smeared the Ka'bah with their blood as an act of drawing near to God Most High, so the Muslims intended to do the same, and this verse was revealed. ﴿Thus He has subjected them to you﴾ (kadhalika sakkharaha lakum) is repeated as a reminder of the blessing and as a reason for what follows in His words: ﴿that you may magnify God﴾ (li-tukabbiru Allah), that is, that you may know His greatness through His power over what no one else can control, so that you may single Him out with grandeur. It has been said that it refers to saying "Allahu akbar" at the time of becoming permitted (from ihram) or at slaughter. ﴿For what He has guided you to﴾ (ala ma hadakum): He guided you to the way of subjecting them and the manner of drawing near through them. The word (ma) may be either a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah) or a relative pronoun (khabariyyah), and (ala) is connected to (li-tukabbiru) because it implies the meaning of gratitude (shukr). ﴿And give good tidings to the doers of good﴾ (wa bashshir al-muhsinin), that is, the sincere in what they do and what they leave undone.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 38:

﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed﴾ against the malice of the polytheists. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans recited ﴿yudafi'u﴾ (He defends), meaning He exerts Himself in repelling (the harm), with the intensity of one who is being contested in it. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous one﴾ in the trust of Allah, ﴿ungrateful﴾ for His blessing, like one who draws near to the idols by means of his sacrifice, so He does not approve of their action nor support them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 39:

.(p-73)

﴿Permission is given﴾ (uniḍina), i.e., it is allowed (rukhkhiṣa). Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the verb in the active voice (al-binā' lil-fā'il), the agent being God. ﴿To those who are fought against﴾ (lilladhīna yuqātalūna), namely the polytheists; the object of permission is omitted because it is indicated by what precedes it. Nafi', Ibn Amir and Hafs read the taʾ with a fatha (yuqātalūna being read as yuqātalūna with the vowel on the taʾ, i.e., lilladhīna yuqātiluhumu al-mushrikūna), meaning: to those whom the polytheists fight. ﴿Because they have been wronged﴾ (bi-annahum ẓulimū), i.e., because they were wronged. They were the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), whom the polytheists used to harm, and they would come to him (ﷺ) from among those beaten and those with broken heads, complaining of their oppression to him, and he would say to them: "Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight," until he emigrated, and then this verse was revealed. It is the first verse revealed about fighting after the prohibition of it in some seventy-odd verses. ﴿And indeed God is able to give them victory﴾ (wa-inna Allāha ʿalā naṣrihim la-qadīr): a promise to them of victory, just as He promised to repel the harm of the disbelievers from them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 40:

﴿Those who have been expelled from their homes﴾: meaning Makkah. ﴿Without right﴾: without any cause that would justify it for them. ﴿Except that they say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾: in the manner of the saying of al-Nabigha:

؎ There is no fault in them, except that their swords, by them, have notches from the clashing of the battalions.

It is also said that the exception is disjunctive (munqati', i.e. not part of the preceding category). ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others﴾: by empowering the believers among them over the disbelievers. ﴿Then would have been demolished﴾: would have been destroyed, by the domination of the polytheists over the people of the religious communities (milal). Nafi' read "difa'" (دِفاع), and Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read ﴿لَهُدِّمَتْ﴾ (لَهُدِّمَتْ) with the lightened form.

﴿Monasteries﴾: the monasteries of the monastics. ﴿And churches﴾: the churches of the Christians. ﴿And synagogues (ṣalawāt)﴾: the synagogues of the Jews; they were so named because prayer (yuṣallā) is performed in them. It is also said that their origin is ṣilwatā in Hebrew (Ibrani), which was Arabicized. ﴿And mosques﴾: the mosques of the Muslims. ﴿In which the name of Allah is much mentioned﴾: a qualifier of the four, or of the mosques specifically, singled out for them as a mark of excellence. ﴿And Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾: those who help His religion. He has fulfilled His promise by empowering the Muhajirun and the Ansar over the chieftains of the Arabs, the Persian kings (akasira) and the Byzantine emperors (qayasira), and by granting them their land and their homes as inheritance. ﴿Indeed, Allah is most Powerful﴾: over their victory. ﴿Almighty﴾: nothing can prevent Him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 41:

﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, perform the prayer, give the zakat, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.﴾ It is a description of those who were expelled, and it is praise before the trial (thana' qabla bala'). It contains evidence for the soundness of the leadership (amr) of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs (al-Khulafa' al-Rashidun), since none other among the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) combined all of these qualities. It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for "those who help Him." ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters﴾, for their final return is to His judgment, and in it is a confirmation of what He promised.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 42–44:**

﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud have denied [their messengers] before them.﴾ ﴿And the people of Abraham and the people of Lot,﴾ ﴿and the companions of Madyan.﴾ This is a consolation (tasliyah) for him (ﷺ): if his people deny him, he is not unique in denial, for these peoples denied their messengers before his people.

﴿And Moses was denied.﴾ He changed the arrangement (nazm) here and made the verb passive, because his people, the Banu Isra'il, did not deny him; rather, it was the Copts (al-Qibt) who denied him. It is also because his denial was more heinous, and his signs were greater and more widespread. ﴿Then I gave the disbelievers respite,﴾ that is, I gave them time until their appointed terms had run out. ﴿Then I seized them; so how was My rejection?﴾ That is, My disapproval of them, by changing blessing into affliction, life into destruction, and habitation into ruin.(p-74)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 45:

﴿So how many a town did We destroy﴾ by destroying its people. The two Basran readers (Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub) read it without the form of emphasis (i.e., ﴿أهلكناها﴾ rather than the plural of majesty). ﴿while it was wrongdoing﴾, i.e., its people were.

﴿So it lies fallen upon its trellises﴾: its walls have collapsed upon its roofs, meaning its structures were rendered idle, so the roofs caved in, then its walls crumbled and fell on top of the roofs. Or it means: empty while its trellises remained intact and sound, in which case the prepositional phrase is connected to ﴿خاوية﴾. It is also permissible that it be a second predicate, i.e., it is empty, and it is upon its trellises, meaning: overlooking them, in that the roofs fell while the walls remained leaning and standing over them. The clause is coordinated with ﴿أهلكناها﴾, not with ﴿وهي ظالمة﴾, for the latter is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the destruction was not the state of its emptiness. So if ﴿أي﴾ (kam-) is in the accusative, there is no place for it (the clause) except by an implied verb that is explained by ﴿أهلكناها﴾; and if you read it in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), then its place is nominative. ﴿and a well left idle﴾: it is coordinated upon (''qarya'', town), i.e., and how many a well, flourishing in the deserts, has been abandoned, none drawing water from it because its people perished. It was also read with the lightened form (ta'khfif) from ''a'tala'', with the same meaning as ''attala''. ﴿and a lofty palace﴾: raised high, or plastered with gypsum; We emptied it of its residents. This strengthens that the meaning of ﴿fallen upon its trellises﴾ is empty while its trellises remain. It has been said that what is meant by "well" is a well at the foot of a mountain in Hadramawt, and by "palace" a palace overlooking from its height, which belonged to the people of Hanzala ibn Safwan from the people of Salih. When they killed him, Allah the Exalted destroyed them and left those two idle.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 46:

﴿Have they not travelled through the land?﴾ This is an exhortation to them to travel so that they may see the ruins of those who were destroyed and take warning (ya'tabiru). Yet although they did travel, they did not travel for that purpose.

﴿So that they may have hearts with which they understand﴾: that is, what ought to be understood of monotheism (al-tawhid) from what they gained through insight (al-istibsar) and reasoning (al-istidlal).

﴿Or ears with which they hear﴾: that is, what ought to be heard of revelation (al-wahy) and of admonition (al-tadhkir) regarding the state of those whose traces they witnessed.

﴿For indeed﴾: the pronoun refers to the matter (al-qissah) or is an undefined pronoun (mubham) explained by "the eyes" (al-absar). The verb ﴿taʿma﴾ (is blind) refers back to it, and the apparent noun has been placed in its position.

﴿It is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blind﴾: that is, regarding consideration (al-i'tibar). The defect is not in their perceptive faculties; rather, their intellects have become blinded by following desire and being absorbed in blind imitation (al-taqlid). The mention of "the breasts" (al-sudur) serves for emphasis and to negate metaphorical usage, and it highlights the warning that real blindness is not the common sense which pertains to the sight.

It was said: when the verse ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world]﴾ was revealed, "Ibn Umm Maktum said: O Messenger of God, I am blind in this world; shall I be blind in the Hereafter?" So the verse ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that are blind﴾ was revealed.

﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ with which they were threatened. ﴿And Allah will not fail His promise﴾, because failing in His report is impossible. So He will afflict them with what He threatened them with, even if after a while. But He is patient and does not hasten the punishment. ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾. This explains the extent of His patience and deliberateness, to the point that He regards long periods as short. Or it refers to the prolonging of His punishment and the actual length of its days. Or it means that the days of hardship seem prolonged. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "you count" with the letter ya' (yā', so that it reads "they count").

﴿And how many a town﴾, meaning "and how many people of a town". The governing noun (al-mudaf, "the noun governed by another") was omitted, and the noun that follows it (al-mudaf ilayh) took its place in i'rab (grammatical case inflection). The pronouns and rulings refer back to the town, for emphasis, generality and awe. He joined the first clause with fa' (fa', "then") and this one with waw (waw, "and") because the first is a badal (badal, "substitution or apposition") for His saying ﴿so how was My denunciation﴾. This clause has the same status as the two clauses preceding it, to show that what they were threatened with will certainly befall them, and that its delay follows Allah's customary way. ﴿I gave them respite﴾ just as I gave you respite. ﴿While it was a wrongdoer﴾ like you. ﴿Then I seized it﴾ with punishment. ﴿And to Me is the final return﴾, and to My judgment is the return of all.(p-75)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 49–51:

﴿Say: O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you.﴾ I make clear to you what I warn you of. The restriction to warning, despite the generality of the address, and the mention of the two groups, is because the beginning and the thrust of the discourse are directed at the polytheists. He mentioned the believers and their reward only as an increase in their rage.

﴿So those who have believed and done righteous deeds – for them is forgiveness﴾ for what has passed from them. ﴿and provision generous﴾ is Paradise, and the [word] "generous" [refers to] every kind whose excellences are gathered together.

﴿And those who strive against Our verses﴾ by rejecting and invalidating them. ﴿seeking to cause failure﴾ competing and opposing those who strive for them through acceptance and verification. It is from ʿājazahu, fa-aʿjazahu and ʿajjazahu, when one competes with him and outstrips him, because each of the two competitors seeks to make the other unable to catch up with him. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read (muʿjizīn) [mu'jizin], as a presumptive circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara). ﴿They are the companions of the Hellfire﴾ the blazing fire; and it has been said that it is the name of a rank (darka) [of Hell].

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 52:

﴿Never did We send before you any messenger or prophet﴾ The messenger (rasul) is one whom God sent with a new law (shari'a) which he calls people to follow. The prophet (nabi) is more general: it includes him and one sent to affirm a previous law, like the prophets of the Children of Israel who came between Musa and Isa, peace be upon them. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ compared the scholars of his community to them. Thus the prophet is more general than the messenger. This is shown by the fact that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about the prophets and said: "One hundred and twenty-four thousand." It was said: "How many of them were messengers?" He said: "Three hundred and thirteen, a great number." It was also said that the messenger is one who, along with a miracle, was given a book revealed to him, while the prophet who has no book is other than the messenger. It was also said that the messenger is one to whom the angel comes with revelation, while the prophet is the term used for him and for one to whom revelation comes in a dream. ﴿Except when he desired﴾ he fabricated in his soul what he wished. ﴿Satan threw into his desire﴾ into his wishing what would require him to be occupied with the worldly life, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed my heart is veiled, so I seek God's forgiveness seventy times a day." ﴿Then God abolishes what Satan throws in﴾ He nullifies it and removes it by His protection, keeping him from inclining towards it and guiding him to what removes it. ﴿Then God makes His verses firm﴾ then He establishes His verses which call to total absorption in the matter of the Hereafter. ﴿And God is Knowing﴾ of the states of people. ﴿Wise﴾ in what He does with them. It was said: he spoke to himself of the removal of poverty, and so this was revealed. It was also said: he desired, out of eagerness for the faith of his people, that there would be sent down to him what would bring them closer to him, and this continued with him until he was in their assembly when the surah (al-Najm) was revealed to him. He began to recite it, and when he reached "And Manat, the third, the other," Satan whispered to him until his tongue slipped inadvertently to say: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is indeed to be hoped for." The polytheists rejoiced at this, until they joined him in prostration when he prostrated at its end, so that no believer or polytheist remained in the mosque without prostrating. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, alerted him, and he grieved over this, so God consoled him with this verse.

This is rejected by the scholars of verification (muhaqqiqun), and even if it is authentic, it is a trial by which the steadfast in faith is distinguished from the wavering. It was also said that ﴿tamanna﴾ means "he recited," as in his saying:

Desiring the Book of God on the first night... as David desired the Psalms with a slow recitation.

His "umniyya" is his recitation, and Satan's throwing into it is that he spoke in such a way, raising his voice, so that the listeners thought it was from the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ. This has also been rejected on the grounds that it undermines confidence in the Qur'an, and it is not removed by His saying ﴿then God abolishes what Satan throws in, then God makes His verses firm﴾, since this too admits of that. The verse indicates the permissibility of error (sahw) in prophets and the occurrence of whispering (waswasa) to them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 53–54:

﴿That He may make what the Shaytan (Satan) casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ This is a reason (ʿillah) for allowing the Shaytan to cast into it, and this indicates that what is cast is a manifest matter, which both the one who is upright (muhiqq) and the one who is in falsehood (mubtil) recognize. ﴿for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ doubt and hypocrisy. ﴿and the hardened of heart﴾ the polytheists. ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers﴾ meaning both groups; the apparent noun was placed in the position of their pronoun as a judgment against them with wrongdoing. ﴿are in extreme dissension﴾ far from the truth, or from the Messenger and the believers.

﴿And that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord﴾ that the Qur'an is the truth sent down from Allah; or, the allowing of the Shaytan to cast is the truth issued from Allah, because it is among the things whose custom He has followed among mankind since Adam. ﴿so that they may believe in it﴾ in the Qur'an, or in Allah. ﴿and their hearts may humbly submit﴾ through submission and fear. ﴿And indeed Allah is the Guide of those who have believed﴾ concerning what is ambiguous ﴿to a straight path﴾ which is a sound reasoning that leads them to what is the truth in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 58–59:

﴿And those who emigrated in the way of Allah, then were killed﴾ in jihad, ﴿or died, Allah will surely provide for them a goodly provision﴾, which is Paradise and its bounties. He made equal between those who were killed in jihad and those who died a natural death in the promise, because the two are alike in intention and in the root of the deed.

It is narrated that some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "O Prophet of Allah, as for those who were killed, we know what good Allah has given them, and we strive alongside you just as they strove. So what will be ours if we die?" Then it was revealed:

﴿And indeed Allah is the best of providers﴾, for He provides without reckoning.

﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance with which they will be pleased﴾, which is Paradise, wherein is what they love. ﴿And indeed Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of their states and the states of their return.

﴿Forbearing﴾, He does not hasten in punishment.

He made equal between those who were killed in jihad and those who died a natural death in the promise, because the two are alike in intention and in the root of the deed.

It is narrated that some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "O Prophet of Allah, as for those who were killed, we know what good Allah has given them, and we strive alongside you just as they strove. So what will be ours if we die?" Then it was revealed:

﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance with which they will be pleased﴾, which is Paradise, wherein is what they love. ﴿And indeed Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of their states and the states of their return.

﴿Forbearing﴾, He does not hasten in punishment.

**﴿That﴾**, i.e., the matter is so. **﴿And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾**, without exceeding in the retribution. The initial punishment is called "retribution" (jaza') only for the sake of pairing (ijtiza', i.e., rhetorical symmetry), or because it is its cause. **﴿Then he is wronged again﴾** by a renewal of the punishment. **﴿Allah will surely help him﴾** without doubt. **﴿Indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾** toward the one who takes vengeance, since he followed his desire in retaliation and turned away from what Allah urged him to by His saying: **﴿And whoever is patient and forgives - indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾**. In this there is an allusion urging pardon and forgiveness, for He, the Exalted, despite His complete power and the exaltedness of His station, pardons and forgives, so others are more deserving of this. It is also a reminder that He, the Exalted, is able to punish, since one is not described as pardoning except one who is capable of its opposite.

ذَلِكَ — That (i.e., that victory).

﴿بِأنَّ اللَّهَ يُولِجُ اللَّيْلَ في النَّهارِ ويُولِجُ النَّهارَ في اللَّيْلِ﴾ — Because Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night.

This is because Allah, exalted is He, is able to make some affairs prevail over others, and His custom is to alternate between opposing things. Among this is the insertion of one of the two alternating periods (al-malawayn) into the other, by which what is lost from one is added to the other, or by bringing the darkness of night into the place of daylight through the setting of the sun, and the reverse of that through its rising.

﴿وَأنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ﴾ — And that Allah is All-Hearing, who hears the speech of the one who retaliates and the one who is retaliated against.

﴿بَصِيرٌ﴾ — All-Seeing, who sees their actions, so He does not neglect them.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ — That: the attribute of perfect power and knowledge.

﴿بِأنَّ اللَّهَ هو الحَقُّ﴾ — Because Allah is the Truth, the one who is established in Himself, the one whose existence is necessary in His own essence alone. For the necessity of His existence and His oneness requires that He be the origin of everything that exists other than Him, knowing Himself and what is other than Himself. Or [al-Haqq means] the one who is established in divinity, and none is fit for it except one who is powerful and knowing.

﴿وَأنَّ ما يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ﴾ — And that what they call upon besides Him [is as a god]. ﴿هُوَ الباطِلُ﴾ — is the falsehood: that which is non-existent in its own essence, or the falsehood of divinity.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 63–64:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ This is an interrogative of confirmation (istifham taqrir), and for this reason it is in the nominative (raf'). ﴿And the earth becomes green﴾ It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿sends down﴾, for if it had been put in the accusative as a response (jawab), it would indicate the negation of greening, as in your saying: "Have you not seen that I came to you so that you honor me?" What is intended is its affirmation. He changed it from the form of the past tense in order to indicate the lasting of the effect of the rain over time after time. ﴿Indeed Allah is Subtle﴾ His knowledge, or His kindness (lutf), reaches everything that is great and everything that is minute. ﴿Aware﴾ of the hidden and the manifest arrangements.

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ in creation and ownership. ﴿And indeed Allah, He is the Free of need (al-Ghani)﴾ in His essence, independent of everything.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 63–64:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ This is an interrogative of confirmation (istifham taqrir), and for this reason it is in the nominative (raf'). ﴿And the earth becomes green﴾ It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿sends down﴾, for if it had been put in the accusative as a response (jawab), it would indicate the negation of greening, as in your saying: "Have you not seen that I came to you so that you honor me?" What is intended is its affirmation. He changed it from the form of the past tense in order to indicate the lasting of the effect of the rain over time after time. ﴿Indeed Allah is Subtle﴾ His knowledge, or His kindness (lutf), reaches everything that is great and everything that is minute. ﴿Aware﴾ of the hidden and the manifest arrangements.

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ in creation and ownership. ﴿And indeed Allah, He is the Free of need (al-Ghani)﴾ in His essence, independent of everything.

﴿the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid)﴾ the one who deserves praise by His attributes and His actions.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 65–66:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is on the earth﴾: He made it submissive to you, prepared for your benefits. ﴿And the ship﴾ is conjoined either to (*mā*, "whatever") or to the noun of (*inna*, "indeed"). It is also recited in the nominative (*marfū'*), as the subject of a new clause (*ibtidā'*). ﴿Running upon the sea by His command﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of it, or its predicate (*khabar*).

﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth﴾: from falling, or out of aversion to its falling, by His creating it in a form inclined to being held up. ﴿Except by His permission﴾: except by His will, and that is the Day of Resurrection. In this there is a refutation of the idea that it holds itself up by its own essence, for it is equal to all other bodies in corporeality, and so it is liable to the downward inclination just as the others are liable to it. ﴿Indeed Allah is, toward mankind, Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾: in that He prepared for them the means of reasoning, opened to them the doors of benefits, and warded off from them various kinds of harm.

﴿It is He who gave you life﴾ after you were inanimate elements (*'anāṣir*) and drops of semen (*nuṭaf*). ﴿Then He causes you to die﴾ when your term comes. ﴿Then He will give you life﴾ in the Hereafter. ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful﴾: he is exceedingly ungrateful (*lajaḥūd*) for the blessings of Allah even though they are manifest.

Or it is because the matter of your religion is too clear to admit dispute. It was also said that the intended meaning is a prohibition to the Messenger (ﷺ) against paying attention to their words and allowing them to engage in debate that leads to contention, for such debate benefits only one who seeks the truth, whereas these people are contentious. Or the meaning is a prohibition against disputing with them, as in your saying: "Zayd will not harm you," and this is permissible only in actions involving contest, because of the mutual implication. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Khuza'ah, who said to the Muslims: "What is the matter with you, that you eat what you have killed yourselves, but do not eat what God has killed?" It has also been recited as **fa-la yan-za'annaka** (﴿so let them not wrench you away﴾), for the purpose of rousing the Messenger and emphasizing his firmness in his religion, on the basis that it derives from *naza'tuhu fa-naza'tuhu*, meaning "I overcame him." **﴿And call to your Lord﴾**, meaning to His oneness and His worship.

**﴿Indeed you are upon a guidance that is straight﴾**, meaning a path leading to the truth, upright.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 72:

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾ from the Qur'an, ﴿clear﴾ manifest in their indication of the true beliefs and the divine rulings.

﴿You will recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve the denial﴾ — the denial, because of the intensity of their rejection of the truth and their rage at the falsehoods they had taken up by blind imitation (taqlid). This is the extreme of ignorance. And to convey this, the phrase "those who disbelieve" was placed in the position of the pronoun, or of what they intend of evil. ﴿They nearly assault those who recite Our verses to them﴾ — they leap upon and attack them. ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that?﴾ — than your rage at those who recite, and your assault upon them, or than the distress that has befallen you because of what they have recited to you. ﴿The Fire﴾ — that is, it is the Fire, as if it were the answer to a questioner who said: "What is it?" It is also permissible for it to be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is: ﴿Allah has promised it to those who disbelieve﴾. It has been read in the accusative (al-nasb) by way of specification (al-ikhtisas), and in the genitive (al-jarr) as an apposition (badal) to "worse" (sharr), in which case the sentence is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), just as when you make it a predicate or a circumstantial clause (hal) of it. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾ — the Fire.

**﴿O mankind, a parable has been coined﴾**: it clarifies for you a strange situation or a remarkable story, and for this reason it is called a *mathal* (parable, likeness). Alternatively, the phrase means "a likeness was attributed to God," i.e., a likeness concerning the entitlement to worship.

**﴿So listen to it﴾**: listen to the parable, or to its matter, with the listening of reflection and contemplation.

**﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides God﴾**: this means the idols. Ya'qub (Yaʿqūb) read *tadʿūna* with the letter *yā'* (i.e., *yadʿūna*, "those they invoke"), and it was also read that way in the passive voice. The returning pronoun to the relative pronoun (*al-mawṣūl*, "the relative") is omitted in the first two readings.

**﴿will never create a fly﴾**: they are not able to create it, despite its smallness, because *lan* (never), with what it contains of emphasis on negation, indicates the incompatibility between the one negated and that from which it is negated. The word *dhubāb* (fly) derives from *dhabb* (driving away), because it is driven away. Its plurals are *adhibbah* and *dhibbān*.

**﴿And if they gathered together for it﴾**: that is, for the act of creating it. The clause *law* (if) with its implied answer is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*), and it is brought for emphasis. That is, they are not able to create it even if they gathered together and cooperated upon it, so how much more so if they were alone.

**﴿And if the fly should snatch away from them anything, they could not rescue it from it﴾**: He made them utterly ignorant by associating with God a god who is capable of all things and who alone brings into existence all that exists, while they are images that are the most powerless of things. He explained this by saying that they are not able to create the smallest and most abject of living creatures, even if they gathered together for it. Rather, they are not even capable of resisting this smallest and most abject creature, nor can they drive it away from themselves or rescue what it snatches from them. It was said that they used to smear them (the idols) with perfume and honey and lock the doors upon them, and the fly would enter through the openings and eat it.

**﴿Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾**: the worshipper of the idol and its worshipped one. Or, the fly seeks what is taken from the idol of the perfume, while the idol seeks the fly to take back from it. Or, the idol and the fly are as if one of them seeks the other, in order to rescue from it what it takes away. And if you examine carefully, you will find the idol weaker by many degrees.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verses 74–76:

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure.﴾ They did not know Him with His true knowing, in that they associated partners with Him and named by His name that which is most remote from Him in fitness. ﴿Indeed, God is All-Strong⁠﴾ over creating all possible things in their entirety. ﴿All-Mighty⁠﴾ nothing overcomes Him, whereas their gods, whom they worship, are incapable of the least of things and are subdued by the most humble of them.

﴿God chooses messengers from among the angels﴾ who act as intermediaries between Him and the prophets, through revelation. ﴿And from among mankind﴾ who call the rest of people to the truth and convey to them what was sent down to them. It is as if, when He had established His oneness in divinity and denied that anything else shares in its attributes, He made clear that He has servants chosen for the message, through whose response and emulation one may be led to the worship of God, glorified and exalted be He, which is the highest rank and the ultimate degree among all existing beings. This affirms prophethood and refutes their saying, ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us nearer to God in closeness﴾, and their claim that the angels are God's daughters, and the like. ﴿Indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing⁠﴾ perceiving all things.

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them⁠﴾ knowing their present and what awaits them. ﴿And to God are all matters returned⁠﴾ all affairs return to Him, for He is their owner in His own essence; He is not questioned about what He does, including His choosing and other things, whereas they will be questioned.
